opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's going to be a really exciting time for programmers, actually, although the nature of the job is certainly going to change. If you look at what these coding systems can already do, writing boilerplate, debugging, translating between languages, scaffolding whole applications from a description, that's moving incredibly fast. In five or ten years I'd expect a lot of the routine implementation work to be handled largely by AI.

But I don't think that makes programmers obsolete. I think it elevates them. The best programmers were never valuable just because they could type syntax quickly. They're valuable because they can decompose a hard problem, understand what actually needs to be built, make good architectural decisions, and have taste about what's elegant and what's going to break. Those skills become even more important when you've got very powerful tools amplifying whatever direction you point them in.

So I think of it a bit like what happened with compilers or high-level languages. People once worried that if you didn't write assembly you weren't really programming. Instead the abstraction level went up, and far more people could build far more ambitious things. I suspect we'll see something similar: one engineer, or a small team, will be able to do what used to take hundreds of people. That's enormously empowering, especially for creative people and for scientists who want to build tools for their own research.

The thing I'd say to young people is: keep learning the fundamentals. Understand how systems work, the maths, the computer science, because you need that to direct these tools well and to know when they're wrong. And at the same time, get really fluent with the AI tools themselves. The people who combine deep understanding with mastery of the new tools are going to be almost superhuman in their productivity. There will be disruption, and we as a society need to take the transition seriously, but on balance I'm optimistic. I think it could be something of a golden era for building things.

r001.rationale: It predicts much higher productivity and mentions the five-to-ten-year horizon, but gives no estimate of roughly ten times productivity.

r002.rationale: It says higher-level tools will let far more people build ambitious things and calls this empowering for creative people.

r003.rationale: It names good architectural decisions as a programmer skill that becomes more important with powerful AI tools.

r004.rationale: It says deep fundamentals help programmers recognize when AI tools are wrong, identifying judgment of their outputs as a continuing skill.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's going to be a fascinating period, and I'd say I'm actually quite optimistic about it, although I don't want to be naive about the disruption.

If you look at what's happened already, these tools have become incredibly good at the kind of boilerplate, the plumbing, the stuff that most programmers would tell you they didn't enjoy that much anyway. So in the near term, the next couple of years, I think what you'll see is that the productivity of good programmers goes up enormously. One person can do what a small team used to do. And that's been true of every tool in the history of computing, really, from compilers to high-level languages to the IDE. Each time people worried it would make programmers redundant, and each time it ended up expanding what was possible, and the demand for software just grew to fill it.

Now, where I think it's different this time is that the systems are going to keep improving, and they're going to move up the stack. So over five to ten years, I'd expect them to go from writing functions to writing modules to eventually taking on fairly complex system design with a human in the loop. And at that point the question becomes, what is the human actually contributing? And I think the answer is taste, judgment, understanding what the problem actually is. Specifying what you want precisely turns out to be most of the difficulty in software, and that's quite a deep skill. It's closer to science or to design than to typing code.

So my advice to someone starting out would be, don't optimise for being a fast coder. Learn the fundamentals deeply, learn to think about systems, about correctness, about what makes a good abstraction. Those things will transfer. And frankly, learn to use these tools as collaborators, because the people who do that well are going to be in a very strong position.

The part I'm less sure about, and I think we should be honest about this, is the entry level. If the junior work is what gets automated first, then how do people acquire the experience to become senior? That's something as an industry we'll have to think about carefully. But overall, I'd rather be a programmer in the next decade than almost anything else, because you're going to have these extraordinary tools and be right at the frontier of what's happening.

r001.rationale: The response predicts a large productivity increase for good programmers, including one person doing the work of a small team, but does not predict roughly tenfold productivity over five to ten years.

r002.rationale: It discusses higher productivity and learning to use AI tools, but does not say that easier coding lets more people with creative ideas implement them.

r003.rationale: It mentions human involvement in complex system design and the value of systems thinking, but does not clearly identify defining software architecture as an expert advantage when using AI assistants.

r004.rationale: The response does not identify evaluating AI-generated code as an expert programmer advantage.

astra-6.text:
I think the nature of programming is going to change quite dramatically. But I’d distinguish between writing code and engineering a system. Writing code is one part of it. Understanding what problem you’re trying to solve, choosing the right abstractions, and knowing whether the result actually does what you intended—those are much broader skills.

Over the next five or ten years, I’d expect AI to take on more of the implementation work. That could allow a small team, or even an individual, to build things that would previously have required a large organization. So there’s an enormous opportunity there. But there will also be disruption, and I don’t think we should pretend we know exactly how the employment picture will work out.

If you’re learning programming today, I would still learn the fundamentals. You need enough understanding to question what the AI produces, especially when it gives you something that looks plausible but contains a subtle mistake. And I’d get comfortable working with these tools.

The interesting question is: when building software becomes much cheaper, how much more software will we want to build? There are so many problems we haven’t tackled because they’ve been too expensive or too difficult. I’m optimistic about that, even if the transition is going to be challenging.

r001.rationale: The response predicts more implementation work will be handled by AI, but does not predict roughly tenfold productivity for top programmers.

r002.rationale: It says an individual or small team may build things that once required a large organization, but does not identify creative ideas as the reason more people can implement them.

r003.rationale: It mentions choosing abstractions, but does not identify software architecture as a continuing advantage of expert programmers working with AI assistants.

r004.rationale: It says people need enough understanding to question AI output, but does not frame evaluating generated code as a continuing advantage of expert programmers.

sol-6.1.text:
I think programming is going to change quite dramatically, but I wouldn’t equate that with programmers becoming obsolete. A lot of the work today involves translating an idea into code, debugging it, and dealing with all the machinery around it. AI can take on more of that, which potentially allows a programmer to be much more ambitious.

The difficult part then becomes: What should we build? Have we specified the problem correctly? How do we know the system actually does what we intended? Those questions require judgment, and they become more important as you can generate more code more quickly.

Five to ten years is quite a long time given how fast things are moving, so I’d be cautious about precise predictions. But if I were learning programming today, I would still learn the fundamentals. You want to understand what the machine is doing well enough to challenge its answers. And I’d get very comfortable working with these tools. There’s an enormous amount of software we’d like to build that we currently don’t have the time or resources to create.

r001.rationale: The response says AI could let programmers be more ambitious, but does not predict roughly tenfold productivity gains over the stated period.

r002.rationale: It says AI may help programmers build more software, but does not identify easier coding as enabling more people with creative ideas to implement them.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention software architecture as a continuing advantage.

r004.rationale: It says programmers will need to judge whether systems do what was intended and challenge AI’s answers, with that judgment becoming more important as code generation increases.
